chapter_theme: The sage ends his account of hell and tells Payapati of the beasts: their one- to five-sensed births and the nigoda below, the tortures men inflict on them, the deceit and hatred that cause a beast's birth, and the deniers sent to the nigoda, then the island peoples counted among animals.

cast.role: King Payapati, addressed by the sage as king, who has turned toward renunciation
the sage who instructs the king; these verses do not name him
those who say there is no soul and no rebirth, as the sage describes them

1955.reading: The sage closes his account of hell: those sunk in its unquenchable fire do not grasp the good teaching, and some who do rise to a better state do not stay there, so nothing more need be said of them.
1955.nuance: It closes the long hell passage (1932 to 1954) and turns, in the next verse, to animal births, so the sarukkam's tour of the bad states runs hell first, then animals, then the island peoples.

claims.claim: some souls who rise to a better state do not remain in it, and those in hell do not grasp the dharma

1956.reading: The sage tells the king to consider the animal births as they multiply, running from the one-sensed up to those that end with the five senses, spread through the good earth.

claims.claim: animal births are graded by number of senses, from one to five

1957.reading: In the long-suffering nigoda births many souls labour having reached only one sense, and a few of them do move out of that state.
1957.nuance: The nigoda is the lowest stratum of Jain life-forms; the verse says only that some leave it, not how or why.

claims.claim: souls in the nigoda state have one sense and suffer, and only some move on from it

1958.reading: One-sensed lives suffer, and few are wise enough to know how they are destroyed, so those of dull understanding kill them.
1958.nuance: Harm is traced to a failure of perception, not to malice: the killers are those lacking sharp knowledge (கூரறிவில்லவர்).

claims.claim: one-sensed beings are killed by those too dull to perceive that they live

1959.reading: Apart from one of the six classes of life, the other named classes of birth are destroyed by people who act as if enraged while the world trembles, without cherishing them.
1959.nuance: Which one of the six classes is excepted cannot be told from the four lines; the verse does not name them.

claims.claim: the classes of living beings are destroyed by the heedless

1960.reading: The remaining moving kinds, from elephants down, are the harmless beasts, and men seize and torment them by force, so that on one side the fat of their flesh runs.
1960.nuance: The suffering is described at its worst in the seizing and cooking of the animal: the line about melting fat (ஊனெய் உருகும்) is the grimmest of the run.

1961.reading: Beasts ridden and loaded with great weights, with legs broken and sinking, are cut and refused and chosen for killing by those who enjoy meat, while some waste away.
1961.nuance: The lines move from the animal as burden-bearer to the animal as meat; the same owner's use and his appetite are laid side by side. Several rare words make the sense of the third line less sure.

1962.reading: Beasts are cut down by the sellers of flesh, crushed by those who cannot stop, and killed by cruel-bowed hunters, so that the animals' pain, the sage tells the king, never lets up.
1962.nuance: Three trades of killing are named in turn: the flesh-seller, the one who breaks the animal, and the hunter. The sage lists occupations that live on animal death, without saying here that each earns its own rebirth.

1963.reading: The sage says that the pitiable beasts look to everyone with their pain, and that even those who stand before them as good people try to be free of them and be done.
1963.nuance: The last two lines are hard to construe: they may say that even people of worth, shown the animals' pain, turn from it rather than help. The reading is a best guess.

1964.reading: The longing of maidens, the sickness that grips even the gods and the burning pain of the suffering animal, the sage says, are known only to ones like himself, so the king should not suppose them small.
1964.nuance: The line pairing the maidens' longing and the gods' sickness with the animals' pain seems to place all three as kinds of suffering, but the third verse line is not clear; the pulli after a vowel sign in line 3 was repaired by the build.

1965.reading: Some animals waste away shrinking from the loud or the foul, and some perish at the hands of cruel people who offer them to deities that take offerings, as the king is told.
1965.nuance: The verse does not argue against sacrifice; it lists it among the ways an animal dies. The Jain objection to offerings is in the choice of that list.

claims.claim: killing animals as offerings to deities is part of the cruelty animals suffer

1966.reading: While mothers rear their young, the young look at them and think of them in love and lie apart or cling, and even so, on one side, they meet countless troubles.
1966.nuance: The verse seems to say that even the tenderness between animal mothers and young does not spare them harm. The construal of line 3 is not secure.

1967.reading: Asking who becomes these suffering beasts, the sage says: those who take up great austerity and afterwards work deceits are born as these.
1967.nuance: The sage names the cause of animal birth as hypocrisy after vows, not as ordinary wrongdoing, so the fault is falling from a state the person had taken up.

claims.claim: those who take up austerity and later practise deceit are reborn as animals

1968.reading: Those who join deceit to wealth, who bewilder others into folly with dark hearts that count none of their own faults, and who lack grace, also become these beasts.

claims.claim: cheating others for gain and lacking compassion lead to animal birth

1969.reading: Those who cling and hate, speak many angers and go out in wrath, and who draw near to what destroys kin, enter the births that these beasts have.
1969.nuance: The third line is hard to construe (the word துவர்ப்பகை is not clear); the verse is read here as stating the causes of animal birth from clinging, hatred and rage.

claims.claim: attachment, hatred and anger lead to animal birth

1970.reading: Sinners who say that there is no soul, no rebirth and no good or evil if one examines it, and who feast on harm, go without pause to the nigoda state.
1970.nuance: The denial is given in the Jain sage's summary and is answered by the penalty it is said to bring, not by argument here; the school is not named, so the view is the sage's account of such deniers, not a statement a materialist would sign.

claims.claim: there is no soul, no rebirth, and no good or bad deed
those who deny soul and rebirth and live by harm go to the nigoda state

1971.reading: Cloud-like generous kings' sons and sky-travelling folk, and many kinds of humans such as the Segar and Milechchar, are counted in the sage's scheme as enjoyers' humans.
1971.nuance: The rare words (சேகர், மிலைச்சர், கடிப்பியர்) name classes of humans in the Jain scheme; I read the verse as a list of human kinds, not as a claim about any one of them.

1972.reading: The ten kinds of the Segar, in the declining age of Bharata and Airavata, lack clear mind, conduct and knowledge, as if their understanding were dead.
1972.nuance: The declining age is named only by the word இழிவு (fall); the verse is a cosmological tag for the kind of human the sage is describing.

1973.reading: Among humans who live in the island lands, those called Milechchar are counted, the sage says, among animals, and beings of that sort die as such.
1973.nuance: The verse ranks a whole people by birth-state; it states the Jain classification and does not argue it. The rest of the passage (1974 to 1977) gives the marks of the class.

claims.claim: island-dwelling Milechchar humans are classed with animals

1974.reading: They have long tails and curved teeth, one leg each, no learning, ears four in number and harmful tusks, lack conduct and live in the island.
1974.nuance: The portrait is of an imagined people at the edge of the world, drawn with marks of beasts; the verse says nothing of real peoples.

1975.reading: Except for the bare fact of human birth they are pale animals, naked, shameless in conduct, gathered on the soil and living by digging and eating earth.
1975.nuance: The verse faults nakedness together with shameless conduct (நாணா ஒழுக்கினர்); it does not say nakedness alone is the fault.

claims.claim: these people are human by birth alone and otherwise animals, for want of shame and conduct

1976.reading: Eating flowers and fruit, many Milechchar live in garden trees, and the sage tells the king to consider that their lives last without end for one palyopama.
1976.nuance: The palyopama is the Jain unit for a vast span of years; the verse gives the lifespan, not the reason for it.

1977.reading: Those joined to the Milechcha lands, though of faultless human form, are of shrinking mind and cruel livelihood, and the sage says that these base ones too he lowers like water.
1977.nuance: The last line (நீச அவரையும் நீரின் இழிப்பாம்) is hard to construe; it is read as a statement that even the human-looking among them are put down.

claims.claim: humans of cruel livelihood and shrunken mind are base though in human form

links.note: 1956 grades animal births by the number of senses from one to five; Neelakesi 77 splits animals into fixed and moving and counts five kinds of the fixed.
links.teaches: The sense-ladder of the Soolamani and the fixed and moving divisions of the Neelakesi are two cuts of one Jain classification of life.

links.note: 1962 names the flesh-seller, the one who crushes and the hunter as the animal's killers; Neelakesi 104 names battle, the chase for food and the nets.
links.teaches: Both Jain tellings draw on one stock list of the animal's torments, so the list is a teaching form and not a poet's own picture.

links.note: 1962 gives the animals' pain at the killers' hands; Siddhar 269 gives the killers' own end, when Death seizes them for the sake of the body's pot.
links.teaches: The Siddhar says the killer will answer to Death, while the Soolamani implies what answering means: birth as the beast he hunted.

gains.a: The animals' sufferings gain a reckoning: the Siddhar shows who comes to answer for them, at death.
gains.b: The Siddhar's threat of Death gains a content: the Soolamani says what follows death, rebirth among the beasts.

links.note: 1965 lists animals killed as offerings to deities among their torments; Kural 259 weighs a thousand oblations against not killing one creature and eating.
links.teaches: The Kural ranks abstention above sacrifice, and the Soolamani shows from the victim's side what the offering costs.

gains.a: The sacrificed animal gains a ranking: the Kural says the rite is worth less than leaving the animal alone.
gains.b: The Kural gains the victim's side: the epic puts the offered animal among the beasts' sufferings, a cost the couplet leaves unsaid.

links.note: 1967 says that those who take austerity and then practise deceit are born as beasts; Kural 274 pictures the false ascetic as a hunter hidden in a bush, snaring birds.
links.teaches: In the Kural the hypocrite hunts the innocent, and the Soolamani turns him into the hunted: the same fault, paid back in the animal's birth.

gains.a: The hypocrite's rebirth gains an image of what he did: the hunter in hiding whom the Kural names.
gains.b: The Kural's hunter gains a sequel: the epic says what becomes of him, since it is the beast's form.

links.note: 1967 sends the false ascetic to an animal birth; Tirumanthiram 1659 sends those of false austerity to hell and says austerities hold only through true knowledge.
links.teaches: Jain and Saiva texts agree that false austerity is punished and differ on the place: a beast's birth in the one, hell in the other.

gains.a: The false ascetic's fate gains a rival account, hell for the Saiva text, that shows the animal birth is a Jain choice.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's hell gains a Jain counterpart in which the punishment is a rebirth that can still be left.

links.note: 1970 sends those who deny soul and rebirth to the nigoda state; Tirumanthiram 2558 sends those who say there is no higher state to hell.
links.teaches: Both texts answer denial with a bad end and not with argument, but one end is a lower birth and the other is hell.

gains.a: The Jain threat gains a Saiva twin, showing that sending the denier to a bad end is a shared habit of polemic.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's denial gains a content: the Soolamani says what is denied, the soul, rebirth and the difference of good and bad.

links.note: 1975 says that a people is human only in the bare fact of birth and otherwise animal for want of shame and conduct; Kural 1071 says the base look just like human beings.
links.teaches: The Kural tests humanness by conduct in each person, while the Soolamani ties the same test to a whole island people's birth.

gains.a: The island people's humanity gains a conduct test: the Kural makes the difference lie in what a person does, not in a land.
gains.b: The Kural's resemblance gains a case where the look-alike is a named people, not a type of person.

links.note: 1973 puts the Milechchar of the islands among the animals; 1977 adds that even those of human form among them, who live by cruelty, are brought down.
links.teaches: The classing with animals in 1973 is widened in 1977 to cover people of human form, so the test shifts from form to livelihood.

new_concepts.gloss: the lowest state of life in Jain teaching, where souls dwell in dense suffering with the fewest senses and from which few rise
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word (1957: நிகோதப் பிறவி; 1970: நிகோத கதி)

source_issues: 1964 line 3 carried a pulli after a vowel sign, repaired by the build.
The words சேகர், மிலைச்சர் and கடிப்பியர் (1971 to 1977) are rare technical terms of the Jain scheme of human kinds, so 1971, 1972 and 1977 are marked uncertain.
1959, 1961, 1963, 1964, 1966 and 1969 turn on hard words or lines and are marked uncertain.
